title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility

paper.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to
billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is
necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE
architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a
500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior
on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features.
Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often
approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas
feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B
BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2% at 5M tokens
to 29% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves
the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction,
whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical
analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the
stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one
feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research. The code can be found on here .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a widely used tool for mechanistic interpretability, aiming to decompose dense model activations into sparse, interpretable features [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . A central motivation is polysemanticity : individual neurons can respond to multiple unrelated concepts, making neuron-level interpretation difficult [ 4 , 5 ] . SAEs address this by learning an encoder that maps activations to sparse latent features and a decoder that reconstructs original activations [ 6 ] . Recent work has scaled SAEs to frontier models such as GPT-4 [ 7 ] and Claude 3 Sonnet [ 8 ] , motivating training on increasingly large collections of activations . This raises a basic question: how much activation data does an SAE actually need? We study this unexplored question in an online training setting by varying activation exposure and measuring two notions of convergence: functional behavior asks how reconstruction and downstream SAE metrics change with activation budget, while feature convergence asks when the learned features themselves become reproducible under one-to-one matching. To clarify the distinction, we develop a theoretical framework of when additional data will lead to feature recovery and show that reducing the amount of activation data alone is not sufficient to guarantee dictionary convergence. This distinction matters because a central motivation for SAEs is not merely good reconstruction but reliable feature discovery. Prior work has questioned whether independently trained SAEs recover the same latent structure [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , with Paulo and Belrose [9] using Hungarian matching [ 12 ] and encoder-decoder agreement to quantify feature correspondence across dictionaries. Our work suggests that large activation budgets are not universally required for high-quality SAE behavior. Our main contributions are: 1) We derive a theoretical characterization of feature recovery under data reduction, and separate statistical consistency from the additional requirements of feature identifiability and successful optimization; 2) across three language models, four SAE architectures, multiple configurations, and activation budgets we present a systematic study of online SAE data requirements; 3) we demonstrate a distinction between functional behavior and feature convergence, where functional SAE metrics exhibit distinct data-scaling behavior, while one-to-one feature reproducibility continues to improve substantially with additional activation exposure; and 4) we show that data selection changes SAE quality in metric-dependent ways: random sampling better preserves reconstruction and intervention-level metrics, while diversity-based sampling shifts training toward high-norm activations and frequently improves Autointerp [ 13 ] . To the best of our knowledge, our findings provide the first systematic evidence that SAE training can be substantially more data-efficient than current large-scale practice. For reconstruction and several functional evaluations, small activation budgets (5M-token) recover much of the behavior of a 500M-token SAE. In contrast, reproducible feature recovery becomes increasingly reliable with larger activation budgets, highlighting SAE’s data requirements depend on the evaluation objective.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Sparse autoencoders and evaluation. Since the standard SAE [ 1 , 2 ] , several architectural variants have been proposed, including JumpReLU [ 14 ] , TopK and BatchTopK [ 7 , 15 ] , and Matryoshka SAEs [ 16 ] . Evaluation has likewise moved beyond reconstruction loss to feature absorption [ 17 ] , sparse probing [ 18 , 7 ] , unlearning [ 19 ] , and automated interpretability [ 20 , 13 ] , which Karvonen et al. [21] compiled into SAEBench, now the standard benchmark for SAE evaluation. Feature stability. A separate line of work asks whether the features SAEs recover are stable. Paulo and Belrose [9] find that SAEs trained on the same data with different seeds learn substantially different features, casting doubt on whether any single SAE identifies a canonical set. Yet Lan et al. [11] show that the spaces these features span remain similar, even across language models. Gerasimov et al. [10] reconcile these findings: Seed-unstable features carry little reconstruction or predictive signal and cluster in reproducible low-rank subspaces, suggesting basis ambiguity rather than noise. We complement this work by asking how feature reproducibility depends on the amount of activation data. Data selection. Outside interpretability, data selection is a well-studied route to efficiency: coreset methods seek a small subset that preserves the training signal of the full dataset [ 22 ] , and Coleman et al. [23] show that cheap proxy models can select such subsets an order of magnitude faster without hurting final accuracy. A common diversity-based strategy is farthest point sampling, which greedily adds the point farthest from the current selection [ 24 , 25 ] and has been applied to core-set selection for deep networks [ 26 ] . Closest to our setting, Yang et al. [27] use SAE features to prune instruction-tuning data, but they select the language model’s training data rather than the SAE’s. We instead ask whether the choice of activations matters beyond their quantity. Research gap: Standard practice trains SAEs on hundreds of millions of tokens [ 21 , 28 ] . To our knowledge, no prior work systematically tests whether this scale is necessary, or whether a selected subset of activations can match SAEs trained on far larger activation budgets on established metrics.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We study SAE data requirements along two axes: activation quantity and activation selection . Unless stated otherwise, we follow the corresponding SAEBench [ 21 ] training and evaluation configurations so that small-data runs are directly comparable to the large-data reference. Models and SAE Configurations. We evaluate three large language models (LLMs) - Gemma-2-2B [ 29 ] (layer 12), Pythia-160M [ 30 ] (layer 6), and Qwen3-8B [ 31 ] (layer 17), and four SAE architectures: BatchTopK [ 15 ] , Matryoshka BatchTopK [ 16 ] , JumpReLU [ 14 ] , and ReLU [ 1 , 2 ] , across multiple configurations. Within each comparison, we hold the LLM, activation site, dictionary width, sparsity setting, and optimization hyperparameters fixed, varying only the activation budget or selection strategy. Online SAE Training. SAEs are trained on FineWeb [ 32 ] in an online activation-generation setting [ 33 ] . Text is streamed through a frozen LLM, target-layer activations are buffered, and SAE mini-batches are drawn from the selected activations before the buffer is refreshed with new text. Selected activations are used once, avoiding a fixed precomputed dataset. Across budgets, we fix the 500 500 M training configuration and optimization steps [ 33 ] , varying only the retained activation fraction to isolate data scale from training exposure. Training-Data Budgets. The reference configuration is designed for 500 500 M activation tokens using [ 33 ] framework. For reduced-data experiments, we retain a fraction q ∈ { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.10 , 1.0 } q\in\{0.01,0.05,0.10,1.0\} of the activations generated at each buffer refresh. Thus, each fresh activation pool contributes 1 % 1\% , 5 % 5\% , 10 % 10\% , or 100 % 100\% of its activations to SAE training. The selected activations are consumed once before a new activation pool is generated from the online data stream. Therefore, q q controls the amount of fresh activation data retained from each online buffer, rather than the size of a fixed replay dataset. Data sampling. We reduce the activation set using two sampling strategies: random sampling and farthest-point sampling (FPS), which explicitly promotes geometric diversity. Evaluation. We evaluate all SAEs using SAEBench [ 21 ] default configurations and metrics, including reconstruction, sparse probing [ 18 , 7 ] , absorption [ 17 ] , SCR [ 34 ] , TPP [ 21 ] , RAVEL [ 35 ] , automated interpretability [ 20 , 13 ] , and unlearning [ 19 ] . We measure feature reproducibility against the 500 500 M reference using one-to-one Hungarian matching of encoder and decoder features [ 9 , 12 ] . Matching similarity and encoder-decoder assignment agreement distinguish feature convergence from functional convergence

sections.heading: 5 Functional Data Requirements Are Metric Dependent
sections.text: Figure 1: Functional data scaling for a BatchTopK SAE with 16 16 k latents. SAEBench metrics are reported for SAEs trained with {5M, 25M, 50M, 500M} activation tokens. While smaller activation budgets approaches the 500M reference for reconstruction, probing, AutoInterp, and intervention-metrics (e, h) exhibit heterogeneous, non-monotonic dependence on activation exposure. Figure 2: Functional data scaling for a standard ReLU SAE with 65 65 k latents. SAEBench metrics are reported for SAEs trained with {5M, 25M, 50M, 500M} activation tokens. Reconstruction remains close to the 500 500 M reference at smaller activation budgets, whereas feature-level metrics show metric-dependent and frequently non-monotonic responses to increasing activation exposure. Here, we show how much activation data is required to reproduce the functional behavior of a large-data SAE. We compare SAEs trained on randomly sampled activation budgets of 5 5 M, 25 25 M, and 50 50 M tokens against corresponding 500 500 M-token references. We focus on two representative configurations: a BatchTopK SAE with 16 16 k latents and a standard ReLU SAE with 65 65 k latents trained on layer 12 residual-stream activations of Gemma-2-2B. Figs. 1 - 2 report the corresponding SAEBench metrics across activation budgets. Results for additional SAE architectures, dictionary widths, and sparsities are provided in Appendix A . a. Reconstruction. The loss measures how well the SAE reconstruction preserves the model’s next-token prediction behavior relative to the original model and a zero-ablation baseline. Observation: The information required for reconstruction is learned early. In Figs. 1 - 2 , we find that all reduced-data SAEs remain close to the 500 500 M reference. While the 5 5 M setting shows only a modest gap, 25 25 M and 50 50 M SAEs are generally very close to the reference, highlighting that substantially less than 500 500 M activation tokens are sufficient to retain the LLM’s behavior captured by SAE reconstruction. b. k k -Sparse Probing (SP). It asks whether a pre-specified concept can be recovered from a small number of SAE latents. Following SAEBench, we report k = 1 k=1 , so the metric specifically probes whether concept information is concentrated in an individual latent. Observation: Concept localization is largely preserved at smaller data budgets. Across sparsity settings and dictionary widths, reduced-data SAEs remain close to the 500 500 M reference. Sparse-probing accuracy is broadly consistent across 5 5 M- 500 500 M budgets, with smaller budgets sometimes outperforming the 500 500 M reference, showing that concept localization is well preserved with substantially less data. c. Feature Absorption (FA). It measures a complementary failure mode: whether a concept that should be represented by its main feature is instead partially captured by other latents. We report 1 − 1- mean absorption; higher is better. Observation: More data does not systematically reduce concept fragmentation. FA is more sensitive to data budget than SP, yet reduced-data SAEs frequently outperform the 500 500 M reference. Together, SP and FA show that strong concept localization and feature alignment can be achieved with substantially smaller data budgets. d. Automated Interpretability. AutoInterp asks an LLM to infer a semantic description of a latent from its activating examples and evaluates whether that description predicts activation on held-out sequences, probing the semantic description of individual features rather than reconstruction quality. Observation: Feature description is not monotonically determined by activation quantity. AutoInterp varies moderately with activation budget, but its ordering depends on SAE configuration, including sparsity and dictionary width. Reduced-data SAEs outperform the 500 500 M reference in many regimes and underperform it in others. In several settings, the trend is even reversed, with smaller activation budgets yielding higher AutoInterp scores. Thus, increasing activation exposure does not consistently improve the semantic description of individual features. e. Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR). It evaluates whether ablating a small set of concept-related latents removes a spurious correlation while preserving the intended classification signal. Observation: SCR shows moderate but non-monotonic sensitivity to data. SCR varies more with activation budget than reconstruction, but increasing data does not consistently improve intervention specificity, and the performance of reduced-data SAEs depends on the width and the architecture. f. Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP). It asks whether ablating latents associated with one class primarily affects that class while leaving others unchanged. Observation: TPP is remarkably insensitive to activation budget Across both dictionary sizes, TPP remains close to the 500 500 M reference despite the large difference in activation exposure. The ordering of data budgets is non-monotonic, but the absolute deviations are small, suggesting that this measure of class-specific feature separation requires relatively little additional data. g. RAVEL. It evaluates whether an intervention successfully changes a targeted attribute while preserving unrelated attributes. Observation: RAVEL is non-monotonic across activation budgets. It varies with activation budget and architecture, indicating that effective intervention can be achieved without requiring consistently larger activation exposure. h. Unlearning. It suppresses latents associated with a target domain and measures whether target knowledge can be removed while unrelated performance is preserved. Observation: Unlearning is the most configuration-sensitive evaluation It varies substantially with activation budget, architecture, and sparsity, highlighting the importance of these factors for unlearning performance. Reduced-data SAEs span a wide performance range relative to the 500 500 M reference, highlighting that effective unlearning can emerge even with substantially smaller activation budgets. To strengthen all the observations above, we additonally add a paired statistical test in Table 26 . In total, these results raise a natural next question: if all other hyperparameters are held constant, are the observed volatile differences primarily a consequence of using less data, or do they also depend on which activations are randomly selected? To separate data quantity from data selection, we next compare random sampling with diversity-based activation selection at matched budgets. Does Data Selection Matter? Here, we ask whether SAE data requirements are determined only by how much data is used, or also by which activations are selected. To separate these effects, we compare uniform random sampling (RS) with Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) [ 24 , 25 ] at matched activation budgets. While RS retains activations independently of their values and therefore preserves the frequency structure of the activation stream in expectation, FPS selects activations to increase geometric coverage, preferentially retaining points that are far from those already selected. We follow the evaluation configuration of Figs. 1 - 2 and compare both selection strategies. Results for additional SAE architectures are reported in Appendix A . Figure 3: Random sampling (RS) vs. FPS for a BatchTopK SAE with 16 16 k latents. At each activation budget, paired bars compare FPS and RS, while the green dashed line denotes the corresponding 500 500 M reference. Selection strategy induces metric-dependent tradeoffs: RS better preserves reconstruction and several intervention metrics, whereas FPS often improves AutoInterp. Fig. 3 shows that the choice of activation subset matters even at a fixed budget: RS and FPS do not produce uniformly better or worse SAEs, but instead favor different properties of the learned representation. i) Random sampling preserves reconstruction . Across dictionary sizes and budgets, loss recovered under RS stays closer to the 500 500 M reference than under FPS, most visibly at small budgets. Geometric coverage alone thus preserves the model’s predictive behavior less faithfully than representative sampling. ii) Concept- and intervention-level metrics favor RS . SCR, TPP, and RAVEL also favor RS across budgets, in some cases exceeding the 500 500 M reference, while SP and FA show no consistent winner. iii) FPS yields higher AutoInterp . FPS outperforms RS on AutoInterp at every budget in both configurations, and in 79% of matched comparisons across all architectures, models, and budgets. FPS shifts training toward geometrically distinct, high-norm activations and is associated with higher AutoInterp but lower reconstruction scores. FPS also outperforms RS on unlearning at some budgets (5M and 50M in Fig. 3 ), though less consistently than for AutoInterp. Data Quality Is Objective Dependent. The matched-budget comparison shows that reducing SAE training data is not characterized by a single notion of data quality. RS better preserves several properties of the full activation stream, most clearly reconstruction, while FPS can improve metrics like AutoInterp and, in some settings of unlearning. Thus, which activations are selected matters in addition to how many are selected. A subset that is representative of the original activation distribution and a subset that maximizes geometric diversity optimize different notions of SAE quality. Why does FPS produce this tradeoff? To characterize what each selector retains, we compared the L2-norm distribution of residual-stream activations selected for SAE training by RS vs. FPS, with all selectors applied to identical activation pools drawn from the 500M-token stream. RS reproduces the stream’s distribution within sampling error at every budget, so its effect is purely a reduction in data quantity. FPS instead concentrates training on a higher-norm region of activation space, shifting the distribution further right as the subset shrinks from 10% to 1% of 500M reference (see Table 1 ). sections.heading: 6 Functional Similarity Does Not Imply Feature Reproducibility
sections.text: So far, increasing activation budget does not uniformly improve SAE function: reconstruction often approaches the 500 500 M reference early, while other metrics remain heterogeneous and non-monotonic. We now ask a stricter question: does functional similarity imply recovery of the same features? Following prior work on SAE feature reproducibility [ 9 ] , we compare reduced-data SAEs against the corresponding 500 500 M-token reference using one-to-one Hungarian matching. Encoder and decoder features are matched independently by cosine similarity. A latent is shared at the threshold τ \tau if both matchings select the same reference latent and both cosine similarities exceed τ \tau . Unless otherwise stated, we use τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 as a strict one-to-one feature-recovery criterion. Counterpart Agreement Emerges Before Strong Feature Recovery. Even at small activation budgets, reduced-data SAEs are not learning completely unrelated dictionaries. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK at 5 5 M tokens, the mean matched decoder cosine similarity is 0.454 0.454 , and independently computed encoder and decoder matchings identify the same reference counterpart for 66.6 % 66.6\% of latents. However, only 2.20 % 2.20\% of latents satisfy the stricter shared-feature criterion at τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 . This gap distinguishes two different notions of correspondence. Counterpart agreement asks whether the encoder and decoder identify the same reference feature, whereas strong feature recovery additionally requires the corresponding feature directions themselves to be highly aligned. Reduced-data SAEs can therefore recover recognizable counterparts well before those counterparts become strongly reproducible. Feature Reproducibility Improves Systematically with Data. Table 2 shows that feature recovery strengthens consistently with activation budget. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, encoder-decoder agreement rises from 66.61 % 66.61\% at 5 5 M to 83.47 % 83.47\% at 50 50 M, while strict shared-feature recovery at τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 increases from 2.20 % 2.20\% to 28.86 % 28.86\% . The same trend holds for ReLU SAEs, showing that counterpart agreement emerges earlier than strong one-to-one feature recovery. Additional results are in Table 25 in the appendix. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we ask a simple but practically important question: How much activation data does an SAE actually need? We study this across four SAE architectures and three language models, analyzing data requirements along three axes: theory, functional performance, and feature reproducibility. First, we develop a theoretical framework characterizing when reduced-data and full-data SAEs should recover the same feature system, showing that convergence to the same population objective is not sufficient for one-to-one feature recovery; identifiability and optimization conditions are also required. Second, training SAEs on 1 % 1\% , 5 % 5\% , 10 % 10\% , and 100 % 100\% of the available online activation data, we find that many SAEBench metrics approach the large-data reference well before the full budget. Third, feature-level analysis reveals a different regime: encoder- and decoder-based Hungarian matchings agree for a substantial fraction of features even at small budgets, but stricter one-to-one similarity criteria show continued improvement with more data. Counterpart agreement thus emerges earlier than strong feature reproducibility. Together, these results suggest that SAE data requirements are objective-dependent. Smaller activation budgets can often preserve reconstruction and aggregate functional behavior, while reproducible recovery of individual features may require substantially more data. We therefore recommend matching SAE training scale to the intended use: avoid defaulting to the largest available activation corpus for functional evaluation, but explicitly assess feature reproducibility when individual latents are used as scientific objects. Limitations. Our study relies heavily on the training and evaluation implementations provided by SAEBench. All functional metrics are computed using the corresponding SAEBench evaluation scripts, and our SAE training pipeline follows the same underlying framework. Consequently, our conclusions inherit any assumptions, implementation choices, and metric-specific limitations of these tools. Additionally, the current SAEBench evaluation framework supports RAVEL and unlearning evaluations only for Gemma models. Consequently, we are currently unable to evaluate the Qwen and Pythia models using these metrics.

Venkatesh Babu Affiliation: Indian Institute of Science Chirag Agarwal Affiliation: University of Virginia Abstract Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2% at 5M tokens to 29% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research. VAL and Aikyam Lab 1 Introduction Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a widely used tool for mechanistic interpretability, aiming to decompose dense model activations into sparse, interpretable features [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . A central motivation is polysemanticity : individual neurons can respond to multiple unrelated concepts, making neuron-level interpretation difficult [ 4 , 5 ] . SAEs address this by learning an encoder that maps activations to sparse latent features and a decoder that reconstructs original activations [ 6 ] . Recent work has scaled SAEs to frontier models such as GPT-4 [ 7 ] and Claude 3 Sonnet [ 8 ] , motivating training on increasingly large collections of activations . This raises a basic question: how much activation data does an SAE actually need? We study this unexplored question in an online training setting by varying activation exposure and measuring two notions of convergence: functional behavior asks how reconstruction and downstream SAE metrics change with activation budget, while feature convergence asks when the learned features themselves become reproducible under one-to-one matching. To clarify the distinction, we develop a theoretical framework of when additional data will lead to feature recovery and show that reducing the amount of activation data alone is not sufficient to guarantee dictionary convergence. This distinction matters because a central motivation for SAEs is not merely good reconstruction but reliable feature discovery. Prior work has questioned whether independently trained SAEs recover the same latent structure [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , with Paulo and Belrose [9] using Hungarian matching [ 12 ] and encoder-decoder agreement to quantify feature correspondence across dictionaries. Our work suggests that large activation budgets are not universally required for high-quality SAE behavior. Our main contributions are: 1) We derive a theoretical characterization of feature recovery under data reduction, and separate statistical consistency from the additional requirements of feature identifiability and successful optimization; 2) across three language models, four SAE architectures, multiple configurations, and activation budgets we present a systematic study of online SAE data requirements; 3) we demonstrate a distinction between functional behavior and feature convergence, where functional SAE metrics exhibit distinct data-scaling behavior, while one-to-one feature reproducibility continues to improve substantially with additional activation exposure; and 4) we show that data selection changes SAE quality in metric-dependent ways: random sampling better preserves reconstruction and intervention-level metrics, while diversity-based sampling shifts training toward high-norm activations and frequently improves Autointerp [ 13 ] . To the best of our knowledge, our findings provide the first systematic evidence that SAE training can be substantially more data-efficient than current large-scale practice. For reconstruction and several functional evaluations, small activation budgets (5M-token) recover much of the behavior of a 500M-token SAE. In contrast, reproducible feature recovery becomes increasingly reliable with larger activation budgets, highlighting SAE’s data requirements depend on the evaluation objective. 2 Related Work Sparse autoencoders and evaluation. Since the standard SAE [ 1 , 2 ] , several architectural variants have been proposed, including JumpReLU [ 14 ] , TopK and BatchTopK [ 7 , 15 ] , and Matryoshka SAEs [ 16 ] . Evaluation has likewise moved beyond reconstruction loss to feature absorption [ 17 ] , sparse probing [ 18 , 7 ] , unlearning [ 19 ] , and automated interpretability [ 20 , 13 ] , which Karvonen et al. [21] compiled into SAEBench, now the standard benchmark for SAE evaluation. Feature stability. A separate line of work asks whether the features SAEs recover are stable. Paulo and Belrose [9] find that SAEs trained on the same data with different seeds learn substantially different features, casting doubt on whether any single SAE identifies a canonical set. Yet Lan et al. [11] show that the spaces these features span remain similar, even across language models. Gerasimov et al. [10] reconcile these findings: Seed-unstable features carry little reconstruction or predictive signal and cluster in reproducible low-rank subspaces, suggesting basis ambiguity rather than noise. We complement this work by asking how feature reproducibility depends on the amount of activation data. Data selection. Outside interpretability, data selection is a well-studied route to efficiency: coreset methods seek a small subset that preserves the training signal of the full dataset [ 22 ] , and Coleman et al. [23] show that cheap proxy models can select such subsets an order of magnitude faster without hurting final accuracy. A common diversity-based strategy is farthest point sampling, which greedily adds the point farthest from the current selection [ 24 , 25 ] and has been applied to core-set selection for deep networks [ 26 ] . Closest to our setting, Yang et al. [27] use SAE features to prune instruction-tuning data, but they select the language model’s training data rather than the SAE’s. We instead ask whether the choice of activations matters beyond their quantity. Research gap: Standard practice trains SAEs on hundreds of millions of tokens [ 21 , 28 ] . To our knowledge, no prior work systematically tests whether this scale is necessary, or whether a selected subset of activations can match SAEs trained on far larger activation budgets on established metrics. 3 When Should Feature Matching Agree? Unless stated otherwise, we follow the corresponding SAEBench [ 21 ] training and evaluation configurations so that small-data runs are directly comparable to the large-data reference. Models and SAE Configurations. We evaluate three large language models (LLMs) - Gemma-2-2B [ 29 ] (layer 12), Pythia-160M [ 30 ] (layer 6), and Qwen3-8B [ 31 ] (layer 17), and four SAE architectures: BatchTopK [ 15 ] , Matryoshka BatchTopK [ 16 ] , JumpReLU [ 14 ] , and ReLU [ 1 , 2 ] , across multiple configurations. Within each comparison, we hold the LLM, activation site, dictionary width, sparsity setting, and optimization hyperparameters fixed, varying only the activation budget or selection strategy. Online SAE Training. SAEs are trained on FineWeb [ 32 ] in an online activation-generation setting [ 33 ] . Text is streamed through a frozen LLM, target-layer activations are buffered, and SAE mini-batches are drawn from the selected activations before the buffer is refreshed with new text. Selected activations are used once, avoiding a fixed precomputed dataset. Across budgets, we fix the 500 500 M training configuration and optimization steps [ 33 ] , varying only the retained activation fraction to isolate data scale from training exposure. Training-Data Budgets. The reference configuration is designed for 500 500 M activation tokens using [ 33 ] framework. For reduced-data experiments, we retain a fraction q ∈ { 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.10 , 1.0 } q\in\{0.01,0.05,0.10,1.0\} of the activations generated at each buffer refresh. Thus, each fresh activation pool contributes 1 % 1\% , 5 % 5\% , 10 % 10\% , or 100 % 100\% of its activations to SAE training. The selected activations are consumed once before a new activation pool is generated from the online data stream. Therefore, q q controls the amount of fresh activation data retained from each online buffer, rather than the size of a fixed replay dataset. Data sampling. We reduce the activation set using two sampling strategies: random sampling and farthest-point sampling (FPS), which explicitly promotes geometric diversity. Evaluation. We evaluate all SAEs using SAEBench [ 21 ] default configurations and metrics, including reconstruction, sparse probing [ 18 , 7 ] , absorption [ 17 ] , SCR [ 34 ] , TPP [ 21 ] , RAVEL [ 35 ] , automated interpretability [ 20 , 13 ] , and unlearning [ 19 ] . Thus, functional similarity can emerge at smaller budgets, while feature reproducibility continues to improve with additional activation exposure, making them distinct notions of SAE convergence. 7 Conclusion In this work, we ask a simple but practically important question: How much activation data does an SAE actually need? We study this across four SAE architectures and three language models, analyzing data requirements along three axes: theory, functional performance, and feature reproducibility. First, we develop a theoretical framework characterizing when reduced-data and full-data SAEs should recover the same feature system, showing that convergence to the same population objective is not sufficient for one-to-one feature recovery; identifiability and optimization conditions are also required. Second, training SAEs on 1 % 1\% , 5 % 5\% , 10 % 10\% , and 100 % 100\% of the available online activation data, we find that many SAEBench metrics approach the large-data reference well before the full budget. Third, feature-level analysis reveals a different regime: encoder- and decoder-based Hungarian matchings agree for a substantial fraction of features even at small budgets, but stricter one-to-one similarity criteria show continued improvement with more data. Counterpart agreement thus emerges earlier than strong feature reproducibility. Together, these results suggest that SAE data requirements are objective-dependent. Smaller activation budgets can often preserve reconstruction and aggregate functional behavior, while reproducible recovery of individual features may require substantially more data. We therefore recommend matching SAE training scale to the intended use: avoid defaulting to the largest available activation corpus for functional evaluation, but explicitly assess feature reproducibility when individual latents are used as scientific objects. Limitations. Our study relies heavily on the training and evaluation implementations provided by SAEBench. All functional metrics are computed using the corresponding SAEBench evaluation scripts, and our SAE training pipeline follows the same underlying framework. Consequently, our conclusions inherit any assumptions, implementation choices, and metric-specific limitations of these tools. Additionally, the current SAEBench evaluation framework supports RAVEL and unlearning evaluations only for Gemma models. Consequently, we are currently unable to evaluate the Qwen and Pythia models using these metrics. References [1] T. Bricken, A. Templeton, J. Batson, B. Chen, A. Jermyn, T. Conerly, N. Turner, C.
